title: Dynamics
lede: Newton's second law with real forces: friction, normal force and slopes. Why trucks lose traction on ice, what holds a load on a grade, and how to solve any force problem with one diagram.

sections.md:
## Free-body diagrams first
Every force problem starts with a **free-body diagram**: draw the object as a dot or box and draw an arrow for **each force acting on it**.

The common forces:

| Force | Symbol | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| **Weight** (gravity) | W = mg | straight down |
| **Normal force** | N | perpendicular to the surface, pushing out |
| **Friction** | f | along the surface, opposing sliding (or the tendency to slide) |
| **Tension** | T | along a rope or chain, pulling |
| **Applied force** | F | whatever direction it's applied |

Then use **Newton's second law** in each direction: **ΣF = ma**. If the object isn't accelerating in a direction, the forces in that direction **balance** (ΣF = 0).

## Weight vs mass, and the normal force
- **Mass** (kg) is how much matter; it's the same everywhere.
- **Weight** (N) is gravity's pull: **W = mg**. A 70 kg person weighs 70 × 9.8 = **686 N** on Earth.

On a flat surface, the **normal force** equals the weight (N = mg), because the floor pushes up just enough to stop you sinking. It's not always equal to mg: on a slope, or if someone pushes down on you, it changes.

## Friction
**Friction** opposes sliding between surfaces. Its maximum size is:

**f = μN**, where μ (mu) is the **coefficient of friction**.

- **Static friction** (μₛ): holds things still. It can be anything up to its max.
- **Kinetic friction** (μₖ): acts while sliding. It's usually **smaller** than static, which is why it takes more force to start sliding a box than to keep it moving, and why a **skidding** tire grips less than a rolling one. That's the idea behind anti-lock brakes (ABS): keep the tires rolling at the edge of grip instead of locking up.

| Tire on road | Approximate μ |
|---|---|
| dry asphalt | ~0.7–0.8 |
| wet asphalt | ~0.4–0.6 |
| packed snow | ~0.2–0.3 |
| ice | ~0.1 |

sections.q: Why do anti-lock brakes help you stop?
options: They keep tires from locking, so static friction (higher) is used instead of kinetic
sections.why: Rolling tires use static friction, which is stronger than sliding friction.

sections.title: Ice vs dry road
sections.problem: The maximum braking deceleration from friction is a = μg. Compare stopping from 20 m/s on dry asphalt (μ = 0.7) and ice (μ = 0.1).
sections.answer: **About 7× farther on ice.** Notice mass cancels out: a = μg doesn't depend on weight, so a heavier truck doesn't stop shorter on ice. (In practice, heavy vehicles also have brake and load-transfer limits that make them stop longer.)

sections.md:
## Slopes: split the weight
On a slope at angle θ, split gravity into two parts:

- **Along the slope**: **mg sin θ** (pulls the object downhill)
- **Into the slope**: **mg cos θ** (balanced by the normal force: N = mg cos θ)

An object stays put if static friction can match the downhill pull: μₛ · mg cos θ ≥ mg sin θ, which simplifies to **tan θ ≤ μₛ**.

*A 10° grade:* sin 10° ≈ 0.17. On a 36,000 kg truck, gravity pulls about 0.17 × 36,000 × 9.8 ≈ **60,000 N** downhill. That's what the brakes or engine must hold back on a long descent.

sections.q: On a slope, the normal force is…
sections.why: Only the component pressing into the surface.

sections.md:
## Solving any force problem
1. **Draw** the free-body diagram.
2. **Choose axes** (on a slope, tilt them along and perpendicular to the slope).
3. **Write ΣF = ma** for each axis.
4. **Solve**, and check units and whether the answer makes sense.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Normal force isn't always mg.** Check the slope and other forces.
- **Friction opposes motion relative to the surface**, not always "backward." Static friction is what pushes a car **forward** (tires push back on the road; the road pushes the car forward).
- **Mass ≠ weight.** kg vs N.
- **Forces on different objects don't go on the same diagram.** Only forces acting **on** your object.

practice.q: Weight of an 80 kg fighter on Earth? (g = 9.8)
Net force to accelerate 1,500 kg at 2 m/s²?
Normal force on a 50 kg box on flat ground? (g = 9.8)
Max friction force: μ = 0.4, normal force 1,000 N?
Usually, compared to static friction, kinetic friction is…
Which surface has the lowest friction coefficient for tires?
A 10 kg box is pushed with 50 N; friction is 20 N. Acceleration?
On a slope, the component of gravity pulling an object downhill is…
Max braking deceleration on wet asphalt with μ = 0.5? (g = 9.8)
A box sits on a ramp without sliding. As you slowly raise the ramp, it starts to slide when…
practice.why: Sliding starts when mg sin θ = μₛ mg cos θ → tan θ = μₛ.
practice.hint: Set the downhill pull equal to max static friction.

practice.q: A 2,000 kg car on a 30° frictionless slope. Downhill acceleration? (g = 9.8; sin 30° = 0.5)
practice.why: a = g sin θ = 9.8 × 0.5 = **4.9 m/s²**. Again, mass cancels.
practice.hint: Divide the downhill force by mass.
